solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: The fridge is rearranged to hold new chicken

indicators.note: the shuffled letters take in the next piece, holding it inside them
the letters of the words the fridge are shuffled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone reorganises the fridge to make room for a freshly bought chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chicken' looks like the food in the fridge, but it is the definition in its adjective sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken as an adjective is slang for cowardly or scared, a synonym.

clue.text: Knock down chap with no exclamation of pain

indicators.note: with no tells us the following item is removed from the word for chap

parts.note: a chap is a fellow
ow is what someone cries when hurt

explanation.surface: A man is knocked over and doesn't even cry out.
explanation.definitionFit: To fell someone or something is to knock it to the ground, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Read Pinter beginning to end and retain only 50%

indicators.note: the first letter of the playwright's name is moved to the end

parts.note: Harold Pinter, the English playwright, taken as written

indicators.note: only half, the front half, of the word retain is kept

explanation.surface: Instructions for studying a Pinter play, perhaps cutting it down by half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to end' moves the P of PINTER to the back, giving INTERP; 'only 50%' keeps RET, half of RETAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To read something such as a situation or a text is to construe or make sense of it.

clue.text: Women's quarters in which are Muslims?

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words which are Muslims

explanation.surface: A question asking whether the women's apartments are the ones occupied by Muslims.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'which', all of 'are' and the start of 'Muslims'.
explanation.definitionFit: In a traditional Muslim household the separate living area reserved for the women bears this name.

clue.text: Attempts loudly to enter English citadels

indicators.note: the letter for loudly goes into the pieces for English citadels

parts.note: citadels are fortresses, or forts
F, forte, is the musical direction for loudly

explanation.surface: An army noisily tries to storm English strongholds.
explanation.definitionFit: Efforts are tries or endeavours, so the plural noun is a synonym of attempts.

clue.text: Organ gang is burning

parts.note: the ear is an organ of hearing
a nest can mean a gang or group, as in a nest of thieves

explanation.surface: Reads like a news snippet about a band of organists on fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests the musical instrument, but it is the body organ.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning in the sense of intense and heartfelt matches earnest, meaning sincere and zealous.

clue.text: Small and close to the ground — like a tortoise?

parts.note: something close to the ground is low

explanation.surface: A description of a tortoise: small and low-slung.
explanation.definitionFit: The tortoise is proverbially sluggish, as in the fable of the tortoise and the hare; the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Fool upset following the Parisian's language

indicators.note: following places the reversed fool after the French article

parts.note: la is French for the, as a Parisian would say it

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means the word for fool is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a nit is a fool, as in nitwit

explanation.surface: An idiot gets in a muddle over French grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue of ancient Rome, still taught in schools and used in law and science.

clue.text: Car in Sweden manufactured without a bit at the front

indicators.note: manufactured says the letters of car in Sweden are worked into something new, without the letter a

explanation.surface: A car built in Sweden lacking a component at the front, perhaps a Volvo.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of CAR IN SWEDEN, 'without' A, are rearranged ('manufactured'). 'Car' looks like the definition, but the definition is 'bit at the front' of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The glass screen at the front of a car is one part of the vehicle, located at its front.

clue.text: Following cattle regularly in both directions

indicators.note: in places the alternate letters of cattle between the two directions

parts.note: L and R, left and right, are both directions

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of cattle

explanation.surface: A cowboy rides behind a herd that keeps wandering back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' picks ATE from cattle, which goes between L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Following as in subsequent or coming afterwards, so the adjective sense of later fits.

clue.text: Out of one's mind?

parts.note: out of one's mind usually means mad, but read literally it is something no longer remembered

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone is insane.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means crazy; taken literally, a thing out of your mind has slipped your memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no longer held in memory has left one's thoughts entirely, so it has been overlooked.

clue.text: Best for female to go in the open air

parts.note: to best someone is to beat or outdo them

indicators.note: to go says the letter for female is dropped from the word for

explanation.surface: A tip on beating a woman at outdoor activities.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdoor describes things done outside, under the open sky, rather than in a building.

clue.text: Shame about detective on television

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Inspector Morse, the Oxford detective of the long-running ITV series

explanation.surface: Someone is embarrassed about a TV detective show.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a much-loved British TV detective drama set in Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Shame and remorse both name the painful guilt felt after wrongdoing, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Cheers, abandoning hot military vehicles

indicators.note: abandoning says the letter for hot is left out of the word for cheers

parts.note: cheers is British slang for thanks
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Soldiers stop cheering and abandon their overheating armoured vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' in British speech commonly means thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanks are armoured, tracked fighting vehicles used by armies.

clue.text: Engineer accepts housing air force rocket, perhaps

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the air force inside them
to engineer is to contrive or rework, so the letters of accepts are rearranged

parts.note: RAF is the Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: An engineer agrees to build a home for the air force, possibly a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like a person, but it is a verb telling us to rearrange 'accepts'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket is one example of a vehicle built for travelling beyond Earth's atmosphere, hence perhaps.

clue.text: Chapters containing King's expressions

indicators.note: containing says the word for chapters holds the letter for king

parts.note: chapters of life are phases or stages
R, for Rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Book chapters full of a monarch's sayings.
explanation.definitionFit: Expressions here are groups of words or turns of speech, which is what the plural noun names.

clue.text: Mariners could make trouble with other ranks on board

indicators.note: on, as in on board a vessel, means placed inside the ship

parts.note: on board is read as aboard a steamship, abbreviated SS
to ail is to trouble or afflict
OR is the military abbreviation for other ranks, the non-officers

explanation.surface: Seamen might cause problems with enlisted soldiers aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is a crossword convention: placing letters inside SS, a steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: Mariners and sailors are both people who work at sea, plain synonyms.

clue.text: Jeans perhaps missing rear pocket

indicators.note: missing rear says the back letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: jeans are an example of trousers

explanation.surface: A pair of jeans lacking the back pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pocket' looks like part of the jeans, but it is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly.

clue.text: Feeling tension developing around South America

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the abbreviation for South America
developing says the letters of tension evolve into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone senses growing tension across South America.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a physical or emotional perception, so it is a synonym of feeling as a noun.

clue.text: Spiteful newspaper extract

definitions.meaning: a spiteful remark is wounding or hurtful
an article clipped from a newspaper

explanation.surface: A malicious piece clipped from the press.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurtful remark is described as sharp or wounding; a clipping from a paper is the same word.

clue.text: Rock climbing in secret in Argentina

indicators.note: climbing says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Covert rock climbing in Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is part of the hidden text; 'climbing' in a down clue means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Granite is a hard igneous stone, an example of rock.

clue.text: Organise a river journey

parts.note: to range is to travel or roam over an area

explanation.surface: Instructions to plan a boat trip.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange something is to set it in order or plan it, a synonym of organise.

clue.text: Seaman oddly seeing crew showing non-attendance

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: oddly takes the odd-placed letters of seeing crew

explanation.surface: A strange sailor watching the crew fail to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seaman oddly' tempts as the odd letters of seaman; 'oddly' acts on 'seeing crew', giving SENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence means not being present, so it is the noun for failing to attend.

clue.text: Cold greeting from Eastender? Bow is appropriate for that

parts.note: a Cockney from London's East End drops the h of hello

explanation.surface: A frosty hello from a Londoner, with a polite bow fitting the occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is also a district in London's East End; here it is the stick drawn across strings.
explanation.definitionFit: The stringed instrument is played with a bow, so a bow suits it.

clue.text: Prison wing exposed in the centre

parts.note: a wing is a limb of a bird

indicators.note: in the centre takes the middle letter of exposed

explanation.surface: A cell block in a jail left open at its middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prison wing' looks like one unit; 'Prison' is the definition and 'wing' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Limbo can mean confinement or imprisonment, a dated slang use for jail.

clue.text: American wearing tiara assembled somewhere in Europe

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are worn around the abbreviation for American
assembled says the letters of tiara are put together in a new order

parts.note: US stands for American, as in United States

explanation.surface: An American tourist tries on a tiara somewhere in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alpine republic with its capital at Vienna is one country in central Europe.

clue.text: Take stock in this bombed church

parts.note: to bomb along is to move fast, so bombed means ran

explanation.surface: A grim invitation to survey the damage in a bombed-out church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take stock' suggests reviewing a situation; the definition reads it literally as livestock held on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: A large farm where cattle or other livestock are raised and kept.

clue.text: The first person singular repeated in confusion

parts.note: me is the first person pronoun

indicators.note: repeated says the letter for singular appears twice

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson tangled up in its own pronouns.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is a state of disorder or muddle, a synonym of confusion.

clue.text: A daughter calling for entry

parts.note: a calling or vocation is a mission in life

explanation.surface: A daughter phones to ask to be let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calling' looks like phoning, but it means a vocation.
explanation.definitionFit: Admission is the act or right of entering a place, so it matches entry.

clue.text: One enthralled by hooter's sound

indicators.note: enthralled by means held captive inside, so the letter for one goes inside the word for hooter

parts.note: hooter is British slang for the nose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone captivated by the honk of a car horn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hooter' suggests a horn, but in British slang it is a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise is any sound, typically a loud or unwelcome one.

clue.text: Blast back and forth

indicators.note: back and forth says the word reads the same in both directions

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A horn sounding repeatedly in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A short blast on a horn or whistle is this word, a synonym.

clue.text: Calls: 'Son, peel the bananas!'

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters of son peel the go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A parent instructs a child to peel the fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit to peel, but it is the slang adjective for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To call someone is to phone them, so the verb forms match.
